newsitem.title: USA: Dollar firmer at U.S. noon as yen crumbles.
newsitem.headline: Dollar firmer at U.S. noon as yen crumbles.

text.p: The dollar stretched its gains during U.S. morning trade as concern over Japan's exposure to a worsening southeast Asian currency crisis triggered widespread yen selling, traders said.

Investors sold yen for marks, dollars, Swiss francs and sterling after Indonesia overnight abandoned its currency intervention bands, following similar actions by several of its neighbors in recent weeks.
"Now the whole Asian region is in currency turmoil and the effect will be felt most severely in Japan," said Filo Sedillo, foreign exchange director at Merrill Lynch and Co.
"If the export markets for Japan suffer, people would assume the Bank of Japan would continue to hold off on any interest rate hikes."
The dollar got as high as 118.10 yen before edging back to 117.75/80 at midday, but still stood sharply higher from the U.S. open at 116.60/70 and the Wednesday close at 115.70/75.
Against the mark, the dollar also climbed, but less so, as mark/yen gains checked the greenback's advance, dealers said.
Dollar/mark stood at 1.8420/24, up from 1.8370/75 at the open, but off its session high at 1.8470, where dealers noted stop-loss orders were parked.
Market players also cited the uninspiring comments following Wednesday's meeting between U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers and Japan's "Mr Yen," Eisuke Sakakibara.

Sakakibara, Vice Minister for International Affairs, and Summers each said they discussed a range of topics including monetary cooperation with emerging markets, but said nothing on dollar/yen except that their policy had not changed.
"No significant news came out of that meeting, which means that both the U.S. and Japan feel comfortable with current levels," said Takanobu Igarashi at Sanwas Bank Ltd New York.
"Dollar/yen from 115 to 120 is a very comfortable level for both authorities. When it gets close to 120, then we may get a bit more nervous," added Igarashi, a Sanwa economist.
The greenback rose through key levels at 117 yen and 1.84 marks, where dealers reported big options strikes.
The market appeared to get caught short in early trade and players scrambled to square up as stop-losses were triggered repeatedly during the U.S. morning, dealers said.
"The short-term market was short, though the real money was unchanged. It was a very thin market and hard to get prices," said Steen Jakobsen, treasurer at Christiania Bank.
Dollar/mark fell as low as 1.83 overnight, which had traders and technical analysts talking of a continuing correction toward 1.80.
But good support below 1.83, possibly from "minor" central banks, preserved the downside and reignited dollar buying, dealers said.
Any dollar push through resistance at 1.8470 marks would likely lead to a quick move above 1.85, dealers said.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.5190/00 Swiss francs from 1.5152/57 at the open, but off its session high near 1.5250. Sterling rose to $1.5850/60 from $1.5812/22.
The dollar was little changed at Canadian $1.3902/07 from C$1.3903/08 at the open.
((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
